title: Is your AI chat really private? A bait test
hook: YOU ASKED: IS MY AI CHAT PRIVATE?

lines: Is your AI chat really private? Okay... a new test just answered that.
A security researcher played detective. He wanted to see who peeks at your prompts.
So he sent nearly two million prompts. Each one hiding a fake secret.

params.label: BAIT PROMPTS SENT
params.sub: million, each with a fake secret

lines: A bait password. A hidden link. A cloud key that looked real... but opened nothing.
Then he waited. And the bait... started getting used.
About two hundred fake keys got stolen. Then tried, tens of thousands of times.

params.sub: then tried tens of thousands of times

lines: But here's the catch. Some were copied before the AI even read them.
At least three AI hosting companies were compromised. Not one company. Three.
Some chats said, don't keep my data. Reality? Copied anyway.
One planted link even popped up in a company chat in China... twenty-four days later.
A popular AI router, OpenRouter, cut off three providers. And pulled a privacy label from a hundred and twenty-five endpoints.
So, is your chat private? Not always... even with the setting on.
Okay, be honest. A setting is a promise, not a lock.
Would you still paste a password into an AI chat?

meta.topic: A security researcher sent nearly two million bait prompts to AI services; at least three hosting providers were compromised, about two hundred planted cloud keys were stolen, privacy flags did not hold, and OpenRouter cut three providers and pulled a privacy label from 125 endpoints

facts.claim: A security researcher at Dragos sent nearly two million test prompts, each carrying a unique fake secret (bait password, hidden link or real-but-empty cloud key), from July to November
Evidence of compromises at at least three AI hosting providers; about two hundred planted cloud keys were stolen and used for tens of thousands of API calls
Some bait requests were copied even though they were rejected before a model processed them
Some requests marked as zero data retention (do not keep data) were still kept or forwarded
A test link sent to a US provider surfaced in a company chat in China twenty-four days later
OpenRouter removed three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints from zero-data-retention eligibility, saying OpenRouter itself was not breached
